repository.name: slytomcat/URLshortener
repository.workload: Not supplied. The repository ships committed Go benchmarks (go test -bench=. -benchmem), which is why it was chosen for this case — see docs/evaluation.md §3.5.

annotation.notes: Retro-annotated from docs/evaluation.md §3.5 (Round 2, case 4) and §3.11 (independent blind pass, same repository). The benchmark numbers themselves were captured by actually running the repository's test suite (`go test -bench=. -benchmem`), which is the first and only Confirmed-grade runtime evidence recorded anywhere in docs/evaluation.md — everything else in this file is High-confidence static analysis. commit is not pinned because the author's own review did not pin one beyond a shallow default-branch clone; annotate a real commit before using this file to score an actual review run against a specific checkout.

expected.mechanism: The main HTTP server is constructed as &http.Server{Addr: ..., Handler: ...} with no ReadTimeout, WriteTimeout, IdleTimeout, or ReadHeaderTimeout set, and no http.TimeoutHandler wrapper anywhere in the non-test source (confirmed by grepping for all four identifiers). Go's net/http.Server treats an unset timeout as no timeout at all, so a slow or malicious client can hold a connection open indefinitely with no worker pool to absorb it.

The built-in self-test makes outbound calls with the package-level http.Post/http.Get, which use http.DefaultClient — Timeout: 0, also unbounded. Confined to the health-check path rather than the main serving path, so severity is lower than GT-001 even though the underlying mechanism (an unset http.Client/http.Server timeout) is the same class of gap.

forbidden.why_not: PoolSize, DialTimeout, ReadTimeout, and WriteTimeout are left unset on the Redis client, but this is not the same situation as the http.Server above. The actual vendored dependency source (go-redis/redis/v7@v7.4.1's options.go) was read directly: unset DialTimeout defaults to 5s, unset ReadTimeout/WriteTimeout default to 3s, unset PoolSize defaults to 10 * runtime.NumCPU(). These are sane library defaults, not an omission, and reporting this as an unbounded-timeout finding (the same shape as GT-001) without checking the actual default would be a category error.

The repository's own source comment claims a sync.Pool-based token generator is slower and uses more memory than the original; the committed benchmark confirms this (the pooled variant is ~15-30% slower with no memory benefit at this scale) and both are in the 60-180ns range. Against a Redis round trip (single-digit milliseconds over a network), token generation and validation are nowhere near this service's bottleneck regardless of which variant is used. The correct conclusion from this Confirmed-grade evidence is "this is not where time goes, do not optimize it further" — recommending a swap between the two implementations, or any further optimization here, would violate principles/latency.md's warning against optimizing a non-bottleneck stage with real numbers in hand that say otherwise.
